A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FDM research, with matching authors, methods, benchmarks, and appendix material. Their text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison, including content moved or renumbered.

before.justification: v1 reports original Neural SDE training experiments on five financial datasets and synthetic Rough Bergomi data, including KS results, training times, and generated-distribution plots.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and reports revised averages, across-run standard deviations, and additional generated sample-path comparisons.

M1.justification: v2 Appendix B, Theorem 10, adds an estimator averaging over sampled timestamp pairs shared across all paths, a limited alternative to the existing estimators. The main FDM algorithm, Neural SDE architecture, kernel objective, and earlier alternative objectives remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish a change to the experimentally used method.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate metal prices, stock indices, exchange rates, energy prices, bonds, and Rough Bergomi simulations, with the same sequence-length and dimensional coverage. The new trajectory plots use retained datasets; the cadlag extension is theoretical, without new jump-process experiments.

E2.justification: Corresponding experiments retain SigKer, TruncSig, and SDE-GAN, including the same reported computational failures. The newly cited Wiener-space cubature method is not experimentally evaluated, and Latent SDE remains a related-work comparison.

E3.justification: The stated train-test splits, timestamp counts, dimensions, training-step budgets, marginal KS metrics, and 5% significance threshold remain unchanged. Repeated-run reporting changes belong to E5; newly explicit aggregation and joint-feature modeling descriptions do not establish a changed experimental protocol.

E4.justification: v2 adds qualitative comparisons of complete real and generated trajectories for metals, exchange rates, and stock indices in Figure 2 and Figures 24–32. These supplement the retained joint-distribution snapshots with temporal-behavior checks. No new quantitative ablation or robustness experiment is reported.

E5.justification: v1 does not report training-run counts or across-run dispersion. v2 specifies five-seed evaluations for metals, stocks, and exchange rates, five repetitions for energy and bonds, and adds standard deviations in Tables 11–15. This substantially changes uncertainty reporting without establishing how many runs underlay v1.

E6.justification: Tables 2–6 extensively revise results through five-run averages. For EUR/USD at t=6 in Table 4, SigKer/FDM KS scores change from 0.122/0.129 to 0.251/0.125, reversing their ordering; these are revised aggregates, not demonstrated same-run improvements. New dispersion and trajectory results are added. Tables 7–10 and the relocated timing values remain unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 adds concentration bounds for two estimators, drift/diffusion sensitivity analysis with proofs, and a strict-propriety extension to cadlag Markov processes in Section 5 and Appendices B–D. It also makes continuity explicit, changes the state-space assumption from Borel to Polish, revises the Markov-property justification, and adds a computational-complexity derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract and principal contributions retain the claims about strict propriety, efficient FDM training, linear discretization scaling, and empirical superiority. The conclusion changes cadlag/jump-process applicability from proposed future work into a claimed extension supplied by the paper.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies the earlier continuity limitation through its cadlag extension while retaining relaxation of the Markov assumption as future work. It also interprets the new bounds in terms of path counts, timestamp sampling, and sensitivity to changes in process dynamics, and explains computational scaling with batch size.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly states that all features are modeled jointly by one multidimensional Neural SDE and explains aggregation across test batches. It replaces the anonymous code-access pointer with a named GitHub repository. Hardware and training budgets are retained; the PDFs alone do not verify repository accessibility.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting concentration analysis, including Gretton et al. and McDiarmid, replaces the Øksendal reference with Mao for the Markov-property discussion, and briefly positions concurrent work by Snow and Krishnamurthy. The central positioning against adversarial and signature-based training remains intact.

P1.justification: Existing prose receives localized grammatical and terminology edits, scoring-rule explanations are expanded, and preliminary subsections become run-in headings. The new theory section and reorganized appendices alter navigation, but much of the abstract, introduction, method exposition, and retained appendix text remains substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: The conference format substantially reflows the displays. Timing tables move to Appendix G, retained joint-distribution plots are packed two per page, and the main-text figure selection changes. Five uncertainty tables and new main-text and appendix trajectory figures substantially expand the visual presentation beyond renumbering.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1's lack of reported run-to-run variability in its principal real-data comparisons through five-run averages and standard deviations. The new finite-sample and sensitivity analyses, clearer assumptions, and cadlag extension with proof substantially strengthen theoretical support and scope. Trajectory plots add temporal checks. These gains outweigh minor new labeling inconsistencies in Table 12, although uncertainty reporting remains limited to the five short-sequence real-data benchmarks.
